summary: ELLIPSE treats a lunar landing site as an ellipse, not a pin. For four representative south-pole sites it computes, over the first 72 hours after a landing date, how many hours each point sees the Sun (by solar disk fraction) and the full Earth, and the longest dark gap. It does this on a 21x21 grid at 50 m spacing around each site centre, using local horizons from NASA LOLA polar elevation models and Sun/Earth directions from NASA JPL SPICE kernels, cross-checked against JPL Horizons. Grid values are combined with Gaussian dispersion weights for sigma 100, 250 and 400 m, and a date-shift view shows how results change if launch slips. A static web viewer shows the precomputed results per site and date as a heatmap, with a table view. The project is a partial prototype: sunlight and Earth-visibility thresholds and the ellipse geometry are not defined, so fraction-of-ellipse values and site verdicts are deliberately shown as not configured. It is a study tool, not a mission planning tool.
details:
What it does

ELLIPSE asks how a landing site's lighting and Earth visibility vary across the area a lander might actually touch down in. For each site it builds a 21x21 grid (50 m spacing, +/-500 m) around the site centre. For every grid point it derives a local horizon from NASA LOLA polar DEMs (20 m and 80 m near field, 240 m far field) and computes Sun and Earth azimuth/elevation every 30 minutes from NASA JPL NAIF SPICE kernels (DE440). From these it reports, for the first 72 hours after each landing date: Sun hours weighted by visible solar disk fraction, full-Earth hours, and the longest dark gap.

How it works

A Python pipeline precomputes everything into JSON files; a static HTML/JavaScript viewer reads them with no server-side code. The viewer shows Gaussian-weighted results for sigma 100, 250 and 400 m, the site-centre reference values and events, a heatmap and table of the 21x21 grid, and an analysis date shift (+N days) for launch slips. The ephemeris implementation was cross-checked against JPL Horizons; because both use JPL development ephemerides, this checks our implementation, not absolute ephemeris accuracy. A horizon sampling diagnostic quantifies the effect of the azimuth step on the results.

Honest limits

No sunlight or Earth-visibility thresholds and no landing ellipse geometry were available from a cited source, and we did not invent them. Fraction-of-ellipse values, required sigma and site verdicts are therefore shown as "not configured". The Gaussian weighting is an isotropic dispersion proxy on the 21x21 support, and the share of the distribution outside the grid is stated for each sigma. Sites are representative points from NASA PGDA, not designated targets. Apollo 11 is listed as unsupported because it lies outside the polar DEMs.

Benefits and impact

It makes the sensitivity of a polar site to landing dispersion and launch slips visible and traceable to public NASA data, so mission concepts can be compared on the same footing once real requirements are supplied.

Tools

Python (spiceypy, rasterio/GDAL, numpy, astroquery, matplotlib), JavaScript, HTML and CSS, Node.js built-in test runner, headless Chrome for layout tests and PDF export, Git.

Creativity and factors considered

Treating the site as a distribution rather than a point, using a date-shift matrix for launch slips, and refusing to show verdicts without sourced thresholds. We considered DEM resolution and extent, horizon sampling, time standards (UTC/TDB), the reference frame (MOON_ME), and accessibility (keyboard navigation and a table alternative to the heatmap).
